messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet remembered the valley not as a landscape but as a sensory trap. The air hung thick with diesel fumes and damp, rotting vegetation, a smell that now clung to him long after the war ended. When the ambush struck, the lead Humvee stalled, its engine coughing into silence before the first rounds cracked the windshield. Stripped of his helmet and soaked through by tropical rain, he felt utterly vulnerable, a raw sense of being naked and exposed against the cold dirt. The relentless purring of passing motorcycles echoed through the tree line, a mechanical rhythm that promised only death. He had never been able to put the frightening event into words; the terror lived in his body rather than his thoughts, refusing to settle into a coherent narrative. Over the years, the moment a motorcycle’s engine growled or the scent of old gasoline drifted past him, Kiet’s breath would catch and his muscles would lock tight. That sudden sensory intrusion always flooded his nervous system with the old conviction that danger was imminent, instantly bridging the trigger to a state of perceived threat. Those same stimuli did more than spike his fear; they dragged him backward into the unspoken footage of the valley. A passing sputter would instantly pull auditory fragments of that day into his head, forcing the past to replay with unrelenting clarity. Because those unbidden recollections arrived with such visceral intensity, Kiet’s baseline anxiety never dropped. The haunting playback of the attack kept his threat system permanently engaged, convincing him that the valley was still only a block away. To keep the relentless replay at bay, he began steering clear of anything that might unspool the tape. He quit his regular running routine, stopped watching the news, and avoided reading anything resembling military accounts, hoping silence would finally quiet the reel. But the more he retreated, the sharper his sensitivities became. By refusing to engage with everyday sounds or physical activity, his nervous system lost the ability to habituate, so a distant engine or a whiff of oil now triggered a full alarm response. His hyper-vigilance, in turn, kept the memories from fading. Because he spent so much energy scanning for danger, his brain never got the chance to process the past as safely concluded, leaving the film running on repeat. That constant state of alertness also made his triggers fire with unnatural frequency. Simply being on guard inside his own house meant that ordinary noises or unfamiliar scents were instantly cataloged as life-threatening signals. At his desk in the open-plan software office, the hum of server racks or the sudden clatter of a dropped keyboard would pull him straight back to the valley. Rather than face those familiar sounds, Kiet routinely worked from his home office, declining client calls and avoiding the office kitchen where a colleague’s cologne or a spilled coffee cup could mimic the ambush’s sensory chaos. Afraid of strangers approaching him at the grocery store, and unable to navigate unfamiliar neighborhoods where he couldn’t gauge exit routes, he found himself isolating, which only deepened his underlying dread. By refusing to leave his apartment or visit places where he couldn’t assess the threat, Kiet inadvertently starved his mind of corrective experiences, allowing the unspoken memories to dominate his waking hours. His avoidance of going out also meant that when he did encounter a trigger, he had no calm memories to counter it, leaving him completely vulnerable to the spike in perceived threat. Now at forty-six, Kiet sat at his screen, the weight of his isolation pressing down. He had come to believe that if he stopped running, the reel would finally stop, but the fear of strangers closing the distance or his own body failing him kept him locked in place. His marriage was fraying under the weight of his withdrawal, and what he hoped for was simply the chance to walk into an unfamiliar room without his heart hammering against his ribs. He was finally seeking therapy because the loop had tightened beyond his endurance.
